Lessons.Title: Represent Data and Solve Problems
ExplanationParagraphs: This Grade 3 2021 first-edition lesson uses REAL data collected from the current class to make picture and bar graphs and solve one- and two-step comparison problems within 20. There is no publisher-approved fixed survey-count answer: counts and, if needed, labels come from a teacher-led sticky-note class poll. Independently authored Edulytics graphs illustrate the task without reproducing the publisher's artwork.

Warm-up — How Many Do You See? (10 minutes): briefly show three different dot arrangements. Learners explain grouping or counting strategies to a partner and compare the images. In the public teacher lesson, the third and second arrangements contain 10 and 8 dots; therefore the third contains 2 more (8 + 2 = 10). The exact pixel grouping of publisher figures has not been inspected, so do not assert a copied arrangement.

Activity 1 — How We Get Home (15 minutes): the teacher collects one real response per child, using a sticky note or an equivalent classroom activity. Suggested categories are bike, walk, van, bus, car and train, but the teacher may adjust categories for that class. Create a picture graph of the ACTUAL responses with a title and a key that one picture equals one student. Then draw a bar graph for the SAME data, label each bar, number the axis and compare the two displays. A teacher checks authenticity and representations; automatic arithmetic must not invent class counts.

Activity 2 — Questions About a Bar Graph (20 minutes): evaluate four statements from the public source in the actual category context: whether walking exceeds every other way; bus exceeds car; walking is fewer than biking; and walking plus biking exceeds van. Record true or false and explain how the class graph supports the decision. Next the teacher selects category names for a one-step 'how many more' question and a two-step 'how many more A or B than C' question. Use actual class counts, show equations and explain thinking. The learning goal is addition and subtraction within 20, not a forced rule that a class can contain at most 20 students.

Lesson synthesis (10 minutes): display a student-created bar graph, invite one- and two-step more/fewer questions, and check each response against the actual class survey. Complete an independent Edulytics Cool-down (5 minutes) on different fictional data; this does not reproduce the publisher's teacher-gated Cool-down. AFTER the Cool-down, allow 2–3 minutes for Math Community discussion about changes to Doing Math/Norms, as described in the publisher's lesson. The storybook suggestion, optional centers, partner reasoning and original figures remain teacher-led or rights-gated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Authentic class data
KeyConcepts.Definition: The picture graph records each classmate's actual response to a category question.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Each surveyed student contributes one answer; do not replace classroom results with fixed figures from the previous lesson.
KeyConcepts.Example: A teacher may choose bike, walk, van, bus, car and train, or adapt the categories for the class.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two matching representations
KeyConcepts.Definition: A picture graph and bar graph can represent precisely the same data using different visual forms.
KeyConcepts.Rule: One picture represents one learner; each bar height must equal the count of the same category, with a clearly numbered axis.
KeyConcepts.Example: If a class poll has 5 walks, both the picture graph and bar graph must show 5 walks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Truthfulness of graph statements
KeyConcepts.Definition: A true/false claim can be checked only from the named class categories and their quantities.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Evaluate each claim against the actual teacher-approved dataset; do not assume walk, bus or any category is most common.
KeyConcepts.Example: 'More walk than bus' is true only when the class's walk count exceeds its bus count.

KeyConcepts.Title: One- and two-step how-many-more
KeyConcepts.Definition: A comparison may require subtracting two category counts, or combining two counts and then comparing.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use the categories chosen by the teacher; compute (A − B) or ((A + B) − C) when they answer the specific more/fewer question; stay within supported arithmetic and explain the interpretation.
KeyConcepts.Example: For a hypothetical example with 5 walkers, 3 bikers and 2 van riders, (5 + 3) − 2 = 6 more walk-or-bike than van.

WorkedExamples.Title: Warm-up — ten and eight dots
WorkedExamples.Question: The third displayed dot image has 10 dots and the second has 8. How many more dots are in the third?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count by grouping and relate the two displayed quantities.
Steps: Count or group the second image to see 8 dots.
Count or group the third image to see 10 dots.
Explain the grouping strategy to a partner; the publisher drawing itself has not been copied.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 1 — construct two graphs from one sample dataset
WorkedExamples.Question: For a FICTIONAL demonstration only, suppose class counts are Bike 3, Walk 5, Van 2, Bus 4, Car 1 and Train 2. How are the picture and bar graphs related?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the same category-to-count mapping for both graphs; do not treat hypothetical data as an authentic class poll.
Steps: Label all six categories in the teacher-chosen order.
For each category draw one independent symbol for each learner and state the key.
Construct one bar per category on an axis starting at zero and labelled in ones.
Check the count of each bar agrees with that picture column.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both displays show Bike 3, Walk 5, Van 2, Bus 4, Car 1 and Train 2; the survey total is 17.
WorkedExamples.Check: 3 + 5 + 2 + 4 + 1 + 2 = 17; each graph uses the same six counts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 2 — decide true or false from supplied counts
WorkedExamples.Question: In the SAME fictional dataset above, is it true that more students walk than any other way, and that fewer walk than bike?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare the specified quantities from the graph, not assumptions about typical transport.
Steps: Find Walk 5, Bus 4, Bike 3, Van 2, Train 2 and Car 1.
Check that 5 exceeds every other single category, so the first statement is true.
Compare Walk 5 and Bike 3; 5 is not less than 3.
Explain both decisions with named data and equations if helpful.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Walk exceeds all other individual categories: true. Walk is fewer than Bike: false.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 2 — teacher-chosen one and two-step questions
WorkedExamples.Question: With fictional counts Walk 5, Bike 3 and Van 2, how many more walk than bike, and how many more walk or bike than van?
WorkedExamples.Method: Choose the categories and compare according to the question, keeping the computation within 20.
Steps: Read the named counts: Walk 5, Bike 3, Van 2.
For the two-step comparison add Walk and Bike: 5 + 3 = 8.
Subtract van from their combined total: 8 − 2 = 6; name the contexts.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 2 more walk than bike; 6 more walk or bike than van.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reusing the previous lesson's six fixed travel counts as if they were this class's real poll.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The 2021 Lesson 2 requires original class data collected with a pupil survey, not the numerical graph from Lesson 1.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Ask the teacher to approve actual responses; if the poll was not performed, label all demonstration numbers as fictional and do not mark source completion.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Changing picture-graph or bar-graph heights when copying the class data.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Two different forms must represent the SAME categorical counts.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Match every category and quantity, use key one symbol = one learner, and check bar heights against a numbered zero-aligned axis.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming the four source true/false statements have universal answers.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Walk, bike, bus and other survey values depend on the actual class.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the current teacher-approved dataset to grade each statement, and separately review the student's explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing more/fewer direction or replacing two-step comparison with a single subtraction.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: For 'A or B than C', two categories must first be combined; a fixed direction matters.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Find the combined group A + B before comparing with C, and state whether it is more, fewer or the same.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Automatically marking teacher-led graph drawing and Math Community reflection correct from a typed number.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: These are visual and interpersonal source tasks with teacher-controlled labels and evidence.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Retain student drawing and open explanation for teacher rubric; independently graded number checks cannot certify those source activities.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up 10 minutes: grouped dot arrangements, including third image 10 versus second image 8 and a difference of 2; partner strategy explanation.
Activity 1 15 minutes: collect real sticky-note class data, then create matching picture and bar graphs with a title, labels, symbol key and numbered scale.
Activity 2 20 minutes: check four actual-dataset true/false claims and teacher-chosen one-step and two-step questions; numeric work is within 20.
Teacher evidence is required for poll provenance, pupil graph creation, question choice, explanation and peer talk; no fixed graph numbers are claimed to be publisher's class data.
Lesson synthesis 10 minutes, separate independent Edulytics Cool-down 5 minutes, THEN 2–3 minutes of Math Community revisions; publisher original Cool-down/image pixels remain unverified.
Optional centers Sort and Display Stage 2 and Capture Squares Stage 3 are not silently replaced by graded numeric questions.
